newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians hail Mubarak, support Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians hail Mubarak, support Arafat.

text.p: Palestinians, sceptical of Israeli intentions to advance peace, hailed Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Tuesday for boycotting a Washington summit and urged PLO leader Yasser Arafat not cave in to Israeli pressure.
But Palestinians justified Arafat's participation in the summit as an attempt to reap political gains for his people.
Mohammed Mbaslat, 31, from the West Bank city of Nablus, said: "I can understand why Arafat had to go. If he doesn't he will be blamed for obstructing peace."
"If Arafat's position is strong, he will get what he wants. There will be a lot of pressure on him and we hope he will stay strong," added Hassan Sider from the West Bank town of Hebron.

U.S. President Bill Clinton called the summit for Tuesday and Wednesday to salvage the Middle East peace process after Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem last week touched off Israeli-Palestinian clashes that killed 72 Arabs and Jews.
Jordan's King Hussein, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat arrived in Washington for the summit. Mubarak declined to attend.

"Mubarak is a hero. His position towards Palestinians and challenging the United States and Israel until they close the tunnel and leave Hebron is honourable," said Ramez Salhab, 32, a shopkeeper in Arab East Jerusalem.
IIhsan Tahboub, 60, a retiree in Jerusalem said:

"Mubarak is a real supporter of the Palestinians. We are very proud of his position because he knows it (the summit) will fail since Netanyahu insisted on his hardline policies even before flying to Washington."
Palestinians said they hoped Arafat would get Israel to close the tunnel, lift a closure imposed on the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip and advance the peace process.
They urged their leader to stand tough.

Arafat hesitated to accept Clinton's invitation when talks between PLO and Israeli officials failed to reach agreement on the summit's agenda. Mubarak told Israeli Maariv newspaper on Tuesday he persuaded Arafat to attend.

Mubarak had linked his attendance to closing the tunnel and Netanyahu's carrying out a troop redeployment in Hebron agreed to by Israel's previous government in an accord signed with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).
Netanyahu has vowed to keep the tunnel open. He wants to renegotiate the Hebron deal. He went to Washington saying he was ready to open continuous negotiations.

Palestinians, glued to their television sets and radios for news on the summit, had mixed feelings. There was a sense of hope leavened with resignation that Netanyahu's hardline policies would lead to the summit's failure.

"We hope Netanyahu understands that Palestinians are boiling and like a volcano they will explode and nothing can put their fire down unless he starts to deal with us as human beings," said Mufid Mustafa, 30, a taxi driver.
"The violence has not subsided, people are waiting to see the summit results."

Before the 1993 PLO-Israel peace deal, Egyptian President Anwar al-Sadat and his successor Mubarak were branded as traitors to the Arab camp by Palestinians for signing a 1979 peace treaty with Israel, the first by an Arab state.
It became the Palestinians' main ally when the right-wing Netanyahu took office last June after ousting Israel's previous centre-left government in May elections.
